# The Estimator Problem {#sec-estimators}

Here is an experiment that costs nothing and changes how you read empirical work.

Take a series of returns. Estimate its tail exponent. Now change one decision — where the fit
starts — and estimate it again. Then change the estimator, keeping the window fixed. Then change
the window again, keeping the estimator fixed.

You will get a set of numbers that differ from each other by more than any of the reported standard
errors. Every one of them was produced by a defensible procedure. If you publish the first one,
you are not lying. You are reporting an artefact of three choices, two of which you will not
mention.

This chapter is about why that happens, what can be done about it, and why the honest answer is
usually less satisfying than the dishonest one.

## What an estimator can get wrong

Textbook treatments separate two sources of error. **Bias** is the systematic distance between what
an estimator returns on average and the quantity it targets. **Variance** is the spread around that
average. The classical trade-off, and the classical fix — more data reduces variance without
changing bias — is the foundation of applied statistics.

There is a third source that the classical framework treats as a specification choice rather than
an error, and it is the one that does the damage here: **window sensitivity.** The estimate depends
on choices made before estimation, such as which observations enter the fit and over what range a
relationship is assumed to hold.

Window sensitivity is a different kind of problem. You cannot reduce it with more data, because the
window is a modelling decision, not a sample. You can only reduce it by reporting it.

| Source | What it is | Reduced by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bias | Systematic offset from the target | Better estimator; correction; different method |
| Variance | Spread across samples | More data |
| Window sensitivity | Dependence on pre-estimation choices | Reporting the choices; testing several |

That third row is why this chapter exists, and why it is placed before the chapters on survival. A
decision procedure that assumes the inputs are precise will fail for a reason that has nothing to
do with the decision procedure.

## Why exponents are worse than means

The ordinary sample mean has a property that exponents do not share. Its error shrinks at a known
rate, and the rate does not depend on unknown features of the distribution, at least to a first
approximation.

Exponents are different, and the reason is where their information lives. A tail exponent is
identified by the largest observations. A long-memory parameter is identified by correlations at
long lags. In both cases, the quantity of interest is carried by a small and shrinking part of the
sample: as you go further into the tail, or further out in lag, there is less data and each point
matters more.

Formally, the effective sample size is far smaller than the nominal one. Informally, the estimate
rests on the handful of observations that make the plot's right-hand tail, and those observations
are correlated with each other in ways that depend on the very structure you are trying to
estimate.

**An exponent is estimated from the part of the data where there is least of it, and where the
usual large-sample guarantees have not yet arrived.**

## What the comparisons found

The systematic comparison of long-memory estimators by Taqqu, Teverovsky and Willinger is the
standard reference on this, and its findings are unflattering to all of the methods it examines:
the estimators carry biases, and the results depend strongly on the method chosen and on the range
of scales included in the fit [@taqqu1995]. I have verified the citation record and the direction
of the finding, not the paper's tables.

Seventeen years later, Franzke and coauthors asked the complementary question: what happens when
the data are not Gaussian? The answer is that the estimators behave differently again
[@franzke2012]. Since financial returns, network traffic, and most natural series are not Gaussian,
this is not a corner case.

The two results together support a generalisation worth stating plainly. **For scale-dependent
quantities, the estimator and the estimation window are part of the result, not part of the
method.** A number without them is not a weaker version of the finding. It is a different claim.

## The same data, two windows

The demonstration is easy to run and worth running once by hand.

Generate a series with a known tail exponent of 1.7 — a value in the middle of the range usually
reported for financial data. Now fit the exponent twice: once using the top five percent of
observations, once using the top one percent.

The second fit will use perhaps a few hundred points. The first will use a few thousand. They will
disagree, and the direction of the disagreement depends on how the far tail deviates from the power
law you assumed.

Now repeat the exercise on a sample of realistic length containing one crisis period. The two fits
will disagree more. The crisis observations will dominate the far-tail fit, and their presence or
absence will move the answer by more than the entire range of exponents reported across markets in
the published literature.

This is the point at which readers usually ask for a rule about which window to use. There is no
such rule, and the request is a symptom of the problem: **if a rule existed, the answer would not
depend on the window.**

## Finding five: what the reporting convention should be

The book's scale-span rule says an exponent travels with its window. That leaves open what to
report when the window cannot be chosen on principle. Three options are available, and they should
be tried in this order.

**Report bounds.** Run the estimate over a grid of windows and estimators. Report the range. This
is honest and it is cheap, and the range is often wide enough to be the finding itself.

**Report the disagreement.** Where a grid is impractical, report the estimates from at least two
methods and say that the difference is not attributable to sampling error.

**Report nothing.** Where the spread is wider than the range of values that would change any
decision, the estimate has no decision content and reporting it invites misuse. Saying "we cannot
measure this reliably enough to act on" is a finding.

The third option is the one most resisted, because it looks like a failure of the researchers. It
is not. It is a report about the identifiability of a quantity, which is a fact about the world and
the data, not about the analyst.

## Identifiability is not uncertainty

The two get treated as synonyms in applied writing, and the difference determines whether more data
helps.

**Uncertainty** is the spread of an estimate that would shrink with a larger sample drawn from the
same process. It is a property of your knowledge. It is about you.

**Identifiability** is whether the data-generating process can be distinguished from its
alternatives given the observations you can obtain. It is a property of the pair, process and data. It is about the world.

A quantity can be uncertain and identifiable: the mean of a well-behaved series is exactly this
case. It can be identifiable and precisely estimated: most parameters in a controlled experiment
are here.

And it can be poorly identified while appearing uncertain, which is the case that causes trouble.
Here the estimator returns a number with a standard error, the standard error is computed correctly
given the model, and both are misleading, because the model's alternatives produce the same data.
**The reported uncertainty is real. It is just uncertainty about the wrong object.**

For tail and memory exponents, the alternatives are not exotic: a power law and a stretched
exponential, a single long-memory process and a short-memory process with a trend, are all
candidates over the spans typically available. That is a statement about identifiability, not about
sample size.

## Why more data does not always help

Two cases are worth keeping apart, because the intuitive remedies differ.

**Case one: the sample is short and the process is stable.** More data helps, at the usual rate.
This is the ordinary case, and the ordinary machinery applies.

**Case two: the sample is long and the process is not stable.** Here more data can make things
worse. Pooling observations from different regimes produces an estimate of an average of exponents,
which corresponds to no regime the analyst will ever face.

The second case is the one that obtains in markets, and it is why long historical samples are less
informative than they look. A hundred years of daily returns contains many regimes. The exponent
estimated across all of them describes a mixture, and the mixture's exponent is not the exponent
that governs the next decade.

**More data does not buy precision when the target is moving.** It buys an average of targets. That is worse than useless.

## A grid protocol, stated so that it can be executed

The previous section recommended reporting ranges instead of points. Here is the protocol, in
enough detail to run.

**Step one: fix the estimator family.** Choose at least two, with different assumptions: for a tail,
a Hill-type estimator and a regression on the upper tail; for memory, rescaled range and a
periodogram method.

**Step two: define a window grid.** For a series with a measurable scale range, choose a set of
lower cut-offs spanning what the data supports — five values is usually enough — and keep the upper
end fixed at the end of the data.

**Step three: compute the matrix.** Every estimator against every window. This costs a few minutes
of computation and produces a table most papers do not contain.

**Step four: report the matrix, or its envelope.** The envelope is the range across the grid, which
is the number with decision content.

**Step five: state whether the decision changes.** Compare the envelope to the range of values that
would alter what you intend to do. If the envelope is narrower, report the midpoint and say why the
spread does not matter. If it is wider, the spread is the finding.

The protocol is not sophisticated. That is deliberate: it can be run by anyone who can fit a line,
and it converts a vague worry about robustness into a table.

## Claim and tool

There is no new claim here about markets. The chapter assembles a result that is familiar to
anyone who has estimated a tail: these quantities are hard to recover from data, and the difficulty
is structural.

The tool, and this is the book's contribution at this point, is to treat estimator and window as
part of the reported object. That has a consequence well beyond tail estimation: it changes what a
finding looks like. A finding is no longer a number. It is a number plus the space of choices that
produced it.

Everything in Part II assumes that inputs arrive in that form. Where they do not, Part II's
procedure is not applicable, and saying so is part of the procedure.

## Boundary conditions

The chapter's argument assumes that exponents are the kind of quantity whose estimate depends on a
window. For quantities with a natural fixed window — a mean over a specified interval, a count in a
defined period — none of this applies, and the ordinary error framework is correct.

It assumes that the process is stationary within the window, which is what makes an exponent a
property of anything at all.

And it does not claim that all estimates are unreliable. It claims that reliability is a property
to be demonstrated rather than assumed, and that for scale-dependent quantities the demonstration
is the grid.

## Two estimators, and what a disagreement means

The book's operational standard for estimability is that two methods with different assumptions be
run and their answers compared. This section says how to run the comparison and how to read the
result, because the practice is more delicate than the standard suggests.

**Choose methods that differ in their assumptions, not in their arithmetic.** Not arithmetic. Two variants of the
same estimator will agree by construction and the agreement will mean nothing. The useful pairs
disagree for a reason: a likelihood fit against a rank-based estimate, a regression on a log-log plot
against a spectral estimate, an estimator that assumes a fixed cut-off against one that selects the
cut-off from the data.

**Report both numbers and the gap.** The gap matters more. The gap is the quantity of interest, and it is more
informative than either estimate. A gap small relative to the effect the decision depends on is a
licence to proceed; a gap of the same order as the effect means the decision cannot be made on this
quantity.

**Read the disagreement in one of three ways, and say which.** The readings call for different
responses.

**Noise.** More data helps. The two methods are sampling the same underlying quantity and differ because both are
imprecise. The response is more data, or a wider interval, and the diagnosis is confirmed by the gap
narrowing as the sample grows.

**Bias.** Find the defect. One method is systematically wrong for reasons that can be identified — a cut-off that
discards information, an assumption that the tail is exactly Pareto when it is not. The response is to
understand which one is wrong, and the diagnosis is confirmed when the biased method's answer moves
toward the other as the known defect is corrected.

**A different object.** Stop estimating. The two methods are not estimating the same thing. This is the reading that
matters most and the one most often missed, and it does not resolve with more data because there is
nothing to converge to.

Chapter 12 supplies the clean example. A power-law fit and a lognormal fit to the same tail can
disagree about the mean — not about its value, about whether it exists — and the disagreement is not
noise, because the two families define different objects. No sample size settles which one the data
came from. **The disagreement is the finding.**

**What to do when the reading is unclear.** Treat it as the third case. Two estimators that cannot be
reconciled by increasing the sample or by correcting a known defect are estimating different objects
as far as the decision is concerned, and the correct response is to bound rather than to point
estimate. **This is the conservative default that the grid of Chapter 14 formalises.**

## Why the standard error is not enough

The estimator comparison is the book's operational test, and the reason a reported standard error does
not substitute for it is worth stating precisely.

**The standard error measures one source of variation.** It describes how much the estimate would move
if the sample were redrawn from the same generating process. It is silent about whether that process is
the right description.

**Three sources it excludes.**
**Model uncertainty.** The estimate's distribution under a different family may be centred elsewhere
entirely, and the standard error computed under the assumed family cannot see this.
**Specification uncertainty.** The cut-off, the window, the treatment of zeroes: choices made before
estimation and rarely reflected in the reported error.
**Regime uncertainty.** Whether the parameter was constant over the sample.

**Why the omission matters more in this material than in most.** Because the quantities this book cares
about — tail exponents, memory parameters, long-horizon edges — are exactly the ones whose estimates
are most sensitive to model and specification choices.

**What to report instead.** The standard error, plus the estimate under a second specification, plus
the estimate on the second half of the sample, plus a sentence on which of the three moved the answer
most. **Four numbers and a sentence is more informative than a coefficient with a standard error in
parentheses, and it is the minimum a decision should be permitted to rely on.**

**Why the convention resists it.** Because a table of coefficients with errors is a format, and a
format is what a review process can request. **The four-number report is a different format, and
adopting it means changing what gets filed.**

## When the two estimators agree

The operational test in this book treats disagreement as informative. Agreement is also informative, and the
mistakes made with it are different.

**What agreement does not establish.** Anything, if the assumptions match. That the estimate is right. **Two methods sharing a common assumption
will agree while both are wrong**, and the assumption is often invisible: a shared cut-off, a shared
stationarity premise, a shared data-cleaning rule.

**Three ways agreement is spurious.**

**Shared specification.** The usual cause. A rank-based and a likelihood estimator applied to the same truncated sample share
the truncation. **The truncation is the assumption that matters, and it is held constant across both.**

**Shared data defects.** Both affected. Both methods use the same records. A reporting convention, a corporate action, or a
survivorship filter affects both identically.

**Insufficient sensitivity.** Agreement by accident. Some quantities are estimated with enough noise that two methods will agree by
accident at small samples. **Agreement at n equals fifty is much weaker evidence than agreement at n equals
five thousand, and the distinction is rarely reported.**

**What to do about it. Two rules.**

**Choose methods that differ where it matters.** Not by algorithm. Where the decision
depends on whether a moment exists, the two methods should differ in their tail treatment specifically.

**Construct the disagreement.** Deliberately. If the two estimators agree, the next step is not to conclude
that the quantity is estimable but to find the assumption they share and vary it. **The third estimate, under
different truncation, is where the information is.**

**Why this section is here.** Because the book's standard is "run two estimators", and a practitioner who
implements the standard mechanically will use two methods that share the assumption they should be testing.
**The test is a comparison of assumptions, not of algorithms.**

## The estimator problem in a regulatory context

The book's material on estimation is addressed to analysts. Its most consequential application is where
estimates become rules, and the setting changes what matters.

**Three features of the regulatory case.**

**The estimate is made public and then fixed.** A capital requirement, a threshold, a limit. **An estimate
revised annually is a different object from one embedded in a rule.**

**The object being estimated responds to the estimate.** Where the rule changes behaviour, the relationship
being estimated changes with it. **This is reflexivity, and it is the analogue of the observer effect in a
setting where the observation is a regulation.**

**The cost of an error is borne by parties who did not make the estimate.** Which changes the burden of proof
rather than the statistics.

**What the estimation analysis implies for regulation. Three rules.**

**Prefer quantities whose estimators agree.** Where two reasonable methods diverge, the quantity should not be
embedded in a rule. **This is the grid's second question used as a design criterion.**

**Report the range and revise on a schedule.** A rule indexed to the estimate rather than fixed at it retains
the ability to adapt without a formal revision.

**Where the quantity is not estimable, use a structure.** A cap, a buffer requirement, a disclosure obligation.
**Structural instruments do not require the estimate to be right, which is why they are preferred where the
estimate is weak.**

**What the chapter contributes here.** The point that a standard error is not an evidential status. **A
regulator who is told that an estimate has a small standard error has been told about one source of variation
and nothing about the other three, and the disclosure that matters is which of the four are quantified.**

## The estimator comparison in four lines

The comparison is the book's measurement standard. Its output in a document is four lines, and the form is worth
stating because the standard is otherwise demanding and vague.

**Line one. The estimate under method A.** With the assumption that distinguishes A.

**Line two. The estimate under method B.** With the assumption that distinguishes B.

**Line three. Which assumption drove the difference.** Not which method is better: which assumption the answer
depends on. **Which is the line that turns two numbers into a finding.**

**Line four. The decision's sensitivity.** What changes if the quantity sits at the low end of the two rather
than at the midpoint.

**What the four lines accomplish. Two things.**

**They make the comparison auditable.** A reader can see which assumptions were varied and re-run the comparison
with a third.

**They connect the estimate to the decision.** The fourth line is the one that determines whether the
disagreement matters at all.

**What the four lines do not include. A recommendation.** Which method to use is a decision that depends on the
setting. **The comparison supplies the disagreement and the sensitivity, and the choice is made by whoever
knows the decision.**

**Why four lines rather than a table.** Because the comparison is usually about one quantity, and a table
implies a set of them. **Four lines beside the number, which is where a reader will look.**

**How to use the lines when the estimates agree.** Report the agreement and state what assumption was shared.
**An agreement between methods with a common assumption is weaker evidence than the four lines make it look,
and the shared assumption is the useful output.**

**What the standard costs.** An hour for the second estimate, and the third and fourth lines are arithmetic. **The
cost is the second estimation, which is why the standard is demanding and why stating its output form makes it
executable.**

## The estimator problem and three sources of disagreement

When two estimators disagree, the source of the disagreement determines the response. Three sources appear in
the material.

**Different estimators. Statistical.** The two methods weight the data differently and would converge with more
of it. **Which is the benign case and the one the comparison is designed to detect.**

**Different assumptions. Specification.** One method truncates at a cut-off the other does not, or assumes a
family the other does not. **Which does not converge with data and requires the assumption to be varied rather
than the sample to be extended.**

**Different objects. Category.** The two methods are estimating quantities that are not the same. **Which is the
case the book's tail-versus-lognormal example illustrates, and it does not resolve at all.**

**What the three require. Increasingly structural responses.**

**Statistical. More data, or a wider interval.**

**Specification. A third estimate under a different assumption.**

**Category. A bound, and a statement of which object the decision needs.**

**How to tell them apart. One test each.** Does the disagreement shrink with the sample. Does it change when a
single assumption is varied. Does the pair of estimates correspond to two different definitions. **Three tests,
each cheap, and the third requires writing the two definitions down.**

**Why the distinction matters for a decision.** Because the first two are about precision and the third is about
reference. **A quantity whose two estimates refer to different objects cannot be made decision-ready by better
data, and the response is a substitution rather than an estimate.**

**What to record. Two items.** The two estimates and the source of their disagreement. **Which is a line and
which tells a reader whether the number in the report is precise, contingent, or about something else.**

## The estimator problem and three ways to report it

The comparison produces two numbers. Three reporting conventions appear, and each loses something.

**The point estimate alone. The most common.** Which conceals the disagreement entirely. **And which is what most
reporting conventions require, since a table of coefficients has one column per quantity.**

**The estimate with a standard error. The statistical convention.** Which reports one source of uncertainty and
implies it is the relevant one. **Which is the failure the chapter names, because the standard error is silent
about the model and the specification.**

**The estimate with its comparison and its sensitivity. The book's convention.** Which reports what the decision
needs and is longer than a table row. **Which is why it is rare and why the chapter's four-line form exists: the
convention has to be short enough to be adopted.**

**What the three lose. Increasingly less.** The first loses the uncertainty; the second loses the specification;
the third loses nothing that is available.

**What the third costs. One row and an hour.** The row is the comparison; the hour is the second estimation.
**Which is the argument for the form: the cost is an hour per quantity, not a research programme.**

**Why the first two conventions persist.** Because they fit a table. **A coefficient with a standard error in
parentheses is a format, and a format is what a review process can request.**

**How to adopt the third without abandoning the format. One addition.** A footnote per quantity giving the second
estimate and the driving assumption. **Which keeps the table and adds the information the decision needs, and it
is the smallest change that a journal or a firm can implement.**

**What the footnote should contain. Two clauses.** The second estimate and the assumption that produces the
difference. **Which is a sentence and which is what the four-line form is for.**

## A note on what this chapter could not check

The two estimator comparisons cited here are described at the level of their records and the
direction of their findings. Their tables were not available to me, and no numerical result is
quoted from either.

The worked demonstration in the middle of the chapter is described rather than shown, because the
figure belongs to the next chapter, where the exercise is set out with its parameters so that the
reader can run it. Nothing in the description depends on the specific numbers, which is the point
of the exercise: the disagreement appears for any parameter choice in the plausible range.
